what: Platform-pack event mnemonics, as data: per config dialect, the syslog mnemonics that record the events a person asks about, each with what it records and the words a question says it with. Two kinds of offer: an event offered "always" (a reload, a restart, an interface or line protocol going up or down, an OSPF or BGP adjacency changing, the configuration changed) is offered for every question, beside the mnemonics the logs reader counted, so an event the range happens not to hold is still named (the operator's walk, 2026-10-26: "Which devices rebooted this week?" was filled with the text "reboot", which IOS never logs); an event offered "named" (a CPU hog, a login) is offered only when the question holds one of its words, because its mnemonic shares no word with how an engineer says it (C1823: "CPU hogs" and "logging in" were offered nothing).
how: Mnemonics as the logs builder carries them (%FACILITY-SEVERITY-NAME), spelled as Cisco's IOS and IOS-XE system message guides give them; %SYS-5-RELOAD, %OSPF-5-ADJCHG, %LINK-3-UPDOWN and %SYS-5-CONFIG_I are also in the lab's Loki (the operator's walk and the logs builder's presets, 2026-10-26), and the named events are each in the lab's captured syslog (tests/fixtures: %SYS-3-CPUHOG in an Explain evidence pack, %SEC_LOGIN-5-LOGIN_SUCCESS in the Loki captures). A reload logs %SYS-5-RELOAD when it is asked for and %SYS-5-RESTART when the system comes back. The words are lower-case and whole: a question holds one when it holds the word itself (each form listed: "hog", "hogs", "hogging"), never a word that merely begins with it, so "logical" is no login. An entry of several words ("logged in") is held when the question has them in that order; one ending in "in" or "on" is not held when a span of time follows it ("logged in the last 30 days" is lines logged, not a login). A word is claimed by one event, or by events that record one happening together (a reload and its restart; an interface and its line protocol; an OSPF and a BGP adjacency), never by a named event and another. No word is "cpu": a CPU figure is a metric, and a CPU hog is said by its own word. Not here: OSPFv3's %OSPFv3-5-ADJCHG until the logs builder takes its lower-case v (C1813); a failed login (%SEC_LOGIN-4-LOGIN_FAILED), which no captured syslog holds, so "failed logins" is offered the login event the pack has; %SYS-5-CONFIG_P and %EVENTLIB-3-CPUHOG, in no captured syslog line.

cisco_ios.records: a reload was requested (the device is about to restart)
the system restarted (logged as it comes back up)
an interface changed state to up or down
an interface's line protocol changed state to up or down
an OSPF neighbour's adjacency changed state
a BGP neighbour went up or down
the configuration was changed (by whom, from where)
a process held the CPU too long (a CPU hog: the process and for how long)
a user logged in (the user, the address they came from and the port)
